Issued at 200 PM CDT Mon Oct 19 2026

A few high cirrus clouds and light southeast winds will result in a 
very pleasant fall evening. Weak WAA overnight will keep our lows 
warm for this time of year, in the low to mid 40s. (Average is mid 
30s) Early Tuesday morning some patchy valley fog is possible, 
especially for areas along and west of the James River Valley. Here 
ensembles indicate a roughly 20-40% probability of visibility 
falling to 2 miles or less. Any fog that forms will be short lived 
and will mix out quickly as winds begin to increase after sunrise.

Tuesday an upper ridge broadens and shifts east over central and 
eastern CONUS. Surface high pressure settles over the Great Lakes 
region, and winds will become southerly. At the same time a mid-
level wave along the western US/CAN border will push southeast. As 
it does so the SPG at the surface will tighten and winds will 
increase and become breezy. By mid-Tuesday afternoon gusts of 15-25 
mph are expected with the highest winds along and west of the James 
River Valley. Occasional gusts up to 30 mph are possible in 
south central South Dakota. The NBM continues to have a low bias
where high temperatures are concerned. After coordination with 
neighbors, boosted highs with a blend of NBM/NBM90. Highs for 
Tuesday are expected to climb into the upper 60s to low 70s, 
with averages for this time of year in the upper 50s to low 60s.


While minimum relative humidity values will remain well above 
critical (near 40% or greater) the warm and dry conditions will 
result in the Grassland Fire Danger Index elevating to the moderate 
category for areas along and west of I-29 Tuesday. The main concern 
for fire will be in the fields themselves as harvesting operations 
continue. Warm, dry, and periodically breezy conditions are expected 
to continue through the week, keeping Fire Danger slightly elevated. 
Please use caution and report any fires immediately.

Early Wednesday morning the previously mentioned wave will drag a 
weak cold front through the region. Guidance has continued to back 
off on rain chances with the front, keeping any rain that forms well 
south of our CWA. Winds will change from southerly to southeasterly 
as the front moves through in the afternoon. Highs for Wednesday 
will again be well above average in the low to mid 70s. 

Through the overnight and continuing on into Friday strong WAA in 
the mid levels will work to sharply amplify the upper ridge. Heights 
aloft will rise to near the maximum of climatology. At the surface 
we can expect clear skies and warm highs in the mid to upper 70s 
both Thursday and Friday. Winds will also be increasing beginning 
Thursday afternoon as a deepening upper trough off the western coast 
moves inland. The tightening SPG will result in afternoon wind gusts 
out of the south-southeast at 15 to 25 mph. Strongest winds will be 
along and west of I-29, with occasional gusts to 30 mph 
possible over central South Dakota. Gusty winds move slowly east
through the overnight and into Friday. By noon widespread gusts
of 25 to 35 mph are possible. Once again the strongest winds 
will be located over central South Dakota where gusts in excess 
of 45 mph are possible. Winds decrease gradually through the 
overnight, but continue gusting 20-30 mph through early Saturday
afternoon. 

By early Friday morning the first wave of vorticity moves into the 
region bringing chances for showers and possibly a few strikes of 
lightning. By Friday evening the main surface cold front will be 
located over central South Dakota, and rain chances increase and 
move east with the it. At this point model divergence is large, and 
too uncertain to try to describe track and timing. Rain totals are 
also very uncertain with ensembles currently showing a 50% 
probability or less of 0.25 inches. Severe weather during this time 
is not anticipated.
